questions.model_answer:
a) Aspergillus fumigatus.
b) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA).
c) (1) Predisposing asthma or cystic fibrosis. (2) Elevated total serum IgE (typically >1000 IU/mL). (3) Immediate skin-test reactivity to A. fumigatus and/or elevated specific IgE/IgG to A. fumigatus. (4) Central bronchiectasis on CT and/or fleeting infiltrates (supportive: eosinophilia >500 cells/µL, precipitating antibodies).
d) Corticosteroids – oral prednisone 0.5–2 mg/kg/day, tapered over 2–3 months.
e) Antifungal therapy with itraconazole (voriconazole or posaconazole if itraconazole fails/not tolerated).

questions.model_answer:
a) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA).
b) Aspergillus fumigatus.
c) (1) Predisposing condition (cystic fibrosis or asthma). (2) Elevated total serum IgE (>1000 IU/mL). (3) Positive Aspergillus fumigatus-specific IgE or immediate (type I) skin-test reactivity. (4) At least two of: precipitating/elevated A. fumigatus-specific IgG, radiographic opacities consistent with ABPA, peripheral eosinophilia >500 cells/uL (in steroid-naive patients).
d) Oral glucocorticoids are the mainstay (e.g., prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day, then tapered over several months), which Mandell notes are reserved for ABPA/asthma in CF.
e) Add an azole antifungal (itraconazole; voriconazole an alternative) as a steroid-sparing adjunct.
questions.beyond_mandell: The chapter names ABPA, A. fumigatus, oral glucocorticoids and itraconazole but does not list the diagnostic criteria; the 4 criteria are from the ISHAM/CF Foundation consensus.

a) Aspergillus fumigatus.
b) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA).
c) (1) Predisposing condition (CF or asthma). (2) Elevated total serum IgE (>1000 IU/mL). (3) Positive A. fumigatus-specific IgE or immediate skin-test reactivity. cohort_answer.text: Organism: Aspergillus fumigatus. Diagnosis: most likely allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) - chronic aspergillosis does not quite fit based on diagnostic criteria. Diagnostic criteria: Predisposing condition (asthma or CF); Increased Aspergillus IgE or Type I hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus skin test; Increased Total IgE (>1000 IU/mL); at least 2 of: increased IgG to aspergillus, radiographic pulmonary opacities consistent with ABPA, eosinophilia >500 cells/uL in steroid-naive patients. Treatment: Systemic glucocorticoids are mainstay (e.g. prednisone 0.5 mg/kg daily x14 days, then every-other-day 0.5mg/kg, taper/discontinue at 3 months; total serum IgE decreases ~25% after 1 month and 60% after 2 months; 35% decrease considered good response). Adjunct: azole antifungal (itraconazole used in studies; voriconazole could be used similarly) - IDSA recommends using both steroids and azoles together.

questions.model_answer:
a) Aspergillus.
b) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) — a long-term allergic (Th2) response to Aspergillus, with an incidence of ~7% in cystic fibrosis.
c) (1) Immediate skin-test reactivity to Aspergillus (or A. fumigatus); (2) Total serum IgE concentration (>417 IU/mL [1000 ng/mL], typically >1000 IU/mL); (3) Elevated serum IgE and/or IgG antibody to A. fumigatus; (4) Serum precipitating antibodies to A. fumigatus. (Supporting: peripheral blood eosinophilia >500 cells/uL, positive sputum culture/hyphae, central bronchiectasis on CT.)
d) Preferred: corticosteroids (oral prednisone 0.5-2 mg/kg/day, max 60 mg/day, for exacerbations, tapered over 2-3 months) — the mainstay. Alternate/adjunct: itraconazole 200 mg/day for 16 weeks, which reduces corticosteroid use, lowers IgE, and improves lung function (voriconazole or posaconazole when itraconazole fails).

cohort_answer.text: a) Aspergillus. b) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). c) Aspergillus serum IgE levels; total serum IgE concentration; elevated Aspergillus IgG; Aspergillus positive precipitin test; Aspergillus positive skin test. d) Systemic steroids + itraconazole for 16 weeks (steroids are mainstay; IDSA 2016 recommends concomitant PO itraconazole to reduce antigenic stimulation and be steroid-sparing; ATS 2009 recommends itraconazole only as steroid-sparing or if not responding to steroids alone).

questions.model_answer:
a) Acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen or Kinyoun) stain and mycobacterial culture, with MALDI-TOF/species identification, given a chalky-white non-branching GPB emerging on antibacterial therapy suggests a rapidly growing mycobacterium.
b) Nontuberculous mycobacterial infection, most likely Mycobacterium abscessus complex.

questions.model_answer:
a) Mycobacterium abscessus complex (a rapidly growing NTM; chalky-white non-branching GPB persisting despite antibacterials).
b) Acid-fast smear (Ziehl-Neelsen/Kinyoun) and mycobacterial culture, with species identification by MALDI-TOF or molecular methods.

cohort_answer.text:
Most likely pathogen: Mycobacterium abscessus (Nocardia would have filamentous branching though)
Next step: AFB + culture. Nocardia would be weakly acid fast. Tx: Imipenem, amikacin, septra. Others: mero/linezolid

parts.text: What is the organism genus and species?
What is the next step in determining the organism?

parts_raw.text: A. What is the organism genus and species?
B. What is the next step in determining organism?

questions.model_answer:
a) Scedosporium apiospermum (Scedosporium apiospermum species complex, formerly Pseudallescheria boydii) — the mold that characteristically colonizes and infects bronchiectatic/cystic fibrosis airways and is selected under trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (which covers both MRSA and Stenotrophomonas).
b) Definitive identification by DNA sequencing, or increasingly by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, of the cultured isolate.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort slide proposed bacterial answers (Burkholderia cepacia complex or Mycobacterium abscessus); as this is the uncommon-fungi chapter and Mandell emphasizes Scedosporium as the CF airway colonizer, the fungal identification is given, but the stem's descriptors ("non-branching, chalky white") are non-specific and the answer is uncertain.

cohort_answer.text: A) Possibly B. cepacia complex (often septra resistant; GNB, rod-shaped, motile, obligate aerobic, matte colonial phenotype; treatable with ceftazidime, meropenem, minocycline, TMP/SMX, FQN, aztreonam, imipenem; most resistant to colistin). Alternate answer: Mycobacterium abscessus (may appear refractile GP/GN rods on Gram stain; non-branching distinguishes from Nocardia; grew in 4 days suggesting rapid grower; CF pathogen; wouldn't respond to stenotrophomonas/MRSA therapy; rapid growers <7 days incl abscessus, fortuitum, chelonae). B) MALDI-TOF; specimens may be stained with Ziehl-Neelsen or modification (Kinyoun) and examined by light microscopy.
